name: Common Cold
info: A mild viral infection of the nose and throat. It is very common and usually clears up on its own within a week to ten days.
medicine_info: General OTC options people commonly use include decongestants, saline nasal spray, and simple pain relievers for comfort. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a pharmacist or doctor before taking anything.
precautions: Rest and get enough sleep
Drink plenty of fluids
Use steam inhalation or a humidifier
Avoid close contact with others to prevent spreading it
Wash hands frequently

name: Influenza (Flu)
info: A contagious viral infection that affects the respiratory system, generally more intense than a common cold and coming on more suddenly.
medicine_info: General fever/pain relief medicine and rest are commonly used for comfort. This is general information only — dosage and choice of medicine should be confirmed with a doctor or pharmacist.
precautions: Rest as much as possible
Stay hydrated
Isolate from others while contagious
Monitor temperature regularly
Use a humidifier for comfort
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath

name: Allergic Rhinitis
info: An allergic reaction causing inflammation inside the nose, typically triggered by pollen, dust, or pet dander.
medicine_info: Antihistamines and nasal sprays are commonly used to manage symptoms. This is general educational information — a doctor or pharmacist should confirm what is suitable.
precautions: Identify and avoid known triggers
Keep windows closed during high pollen periods
Use air purifiers if available
Wash bedding regularly
Rinse nasal passages with saline
warning_signs: Swelling of face, lips, or throat

name: Migraine
info: A neurological condition causing intense, often throbbing headaches, usually on one side of the head, sometimes preceded by visual disturbances.
medicine_info: General pain relief may help mild episodes. This is general information only, not a personalized treatment plan — a doctor should be consulted for recurring migraines.
precautions: Rest in a quiet, dark room
Stay hydrated
Track and avoid personal triggers (certain foods, stress, lack of sleep)
Maintain a regular sleep schedule
warning_signs: Sudden, extremely severe headache unlike previous ones
Headache with fever and stiff neck

name: Gastritis
info: Inflammation of the stomach lining, which can cause discomfort, bloating, and nausea, often linked to diet, stress, or infection.
medicine_info: Antacids are commonly used for temporary relief. This is general information only — a doctor should evaluate persistent stomach issues.
precautions: Eat smaller, more frequent meals
Avoid spicy, oily, or acidic foods
Avoid alcohol and smoking
Avoid lying down immediately after eating
warning_signs: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds

name: Food Poisoning
info: An illness caused by eating contaminated food, usually leading to digestive symptoms that begin within hours to a few days of eating.
medicine_info: Oral rehydration solutions are generally recommended to prevent dehydration. This is general information only — a doctor should be consulted if symptoms are severe or prolonged.
precautions: Drink oral rehydration solution or clear fluids
Rest and avoid solid food until nausea eases
Reintroduce bland food gradually (rice, toast, bananas)
Maintain good hand and food hygiene
warning_signs: Signs of severe dehydration (very little urination, dizziness)

name: Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye)
info: Inflammation of the thin membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelid, often caused by infection or allergy, commonly known as pink eye.
medicine_info: Lubricating eye drops may relieve discomfort. This is general information only — an eye specialist should confirm treatment, especially since some types are contagious.
precautions: Avoid touching or rubbing the eyes
Wash hands frequently
Do not share towels, pillows, or eye makeup
Use a clean, cool compress for comfort
warning_signs: Symptoms not improving after a few days

name: Skin Allergy (Contact Dermatitis / Urticaria)
info: A reaction of the skin to an irritant or allergen, resulting in redness, itching, or raised bumps.
medicine_info: Antihistamines or soothing lotions are commonly used for mild reactions. This is general information only — a doctor should evaluate persistent or severe skin reactions.
precautions: Identify and avoid the triggering substance
Keep the affected area clean and dry
Avoid scratching the area
Use mild, fragrance-free soap and moisturizer
warning_signs: Swelling of the face, lips, or throat

name: Sinusitis
info: Inflammation or swelling of the tissue lining the sinuses, often following a cold, leading to pressure and congestion around the face.
medicine_info: Decongestants and saline rinses are commonly used for relief. This is general information only — a doctor should be consulted if symptoms persist beyond 10 days.
precautions: Use steam inhalation for congestion relief
Stay hydrated to thin mucus
Use a saline nasal rinse
Avoid allergens and irritants like smoke
warning_signs: Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement

name: Sore Throat (Pharyngitis)
info: Inflammation of the throat, commonly caused by a viral infection, resulting in pain or irritation especially when swallowing.
medicine_info: Warm salt water gargles and throat lozenges are commonly used for comfort. This is general information only — a doctor should evaluate a throat infection that does not improve.
precautions: Gargle with warm salt water
Drink warm fluids
Rest the voice
Use a humidifier
warning_signs: Symptoms lasting more than a week

name: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
info: An infection affecting any part of the urinary system, most commonly the bladder, causing discomfort during urination.
medicine_info: This condition typically needs a doctor's evaluation, as it's often treated with a prescribed antibiotic course. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics.
precautions: Drink plenty of water
Urinate frequently and avoid holding it in
Maintain good hygiene
Avoid irritants like harsh soaps in the genital area
warning_signs: Nausea and vomiting alongside urinary symptoms

name: Tension Headache
info: The most common type of headache, often described as a constant dull ache or tightness on both sides of the head, frequently linked to stress or posture.
medicine_info: General pain relievers may provide temporary relief. This is general information only — frequent headaches should be discussed with a doctor.
precautions: Take short breaks from screens
Practice relaxation or stress-reduction techniques
Maintain good posture
Stay hydrated and keep a regular sleep schedule
warning_signs: Sudden, severe headache unlike any before
Headache with fever, stiff neck, or confusion

name: Dehydration
info: A condition that occurs when the body loses more fluids than it takes in, affecting normal bodily functions.
medicine_info: Oral rehydration solutions or water with electrolytes are generally recommended. This is general information only — severe dehydration needs medical attention.
precautions: Drink water or oral rehydration solution steadily through the day
Avoid excess caffeine and alcohol
Rest in a cool environment
Increase fluids further in hot weather or during illness
warning_signs: Little or no urination for many hours
Sunken eyes or extreme dizziness on standing

name: Type 2 Diabetes
info: A long-term condition in which the body cannot use insulin properly, so blood sugar stays high. It is very common, often develops slowly, and can be controlled with diet, exercise and medicines.
medicine_info: Diabetes is managed with doctor-prescribed tablets and/or insulin after blood tests. Never start, stop or change a dose on your own. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get a blood sugar test (fasting and post-meal, HbA1c) done
Choose whole grains, vegetables and fewer sugary foods and sweets
Walk or exercise regularly (about 30 minutes most days)
Keep a healthy weight and check your feet daily for cuts
Take prescribed medicines on time and go for regular check-ups
warning_signs: Very high thirst with vomiting or fruity-smelling breath
Wounds or foot sores that are not healing
Chest pain or sudden weakness on one side

name: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure)
info: A condition where the force of blood against artery walls stays too high. It often has no symptoms at all, which is why regular BP checks matter; left untreated it can damage the heart, brain and kidneys.
medicine_info: Blood pressure is controlled with doctor-prescribed medicines plus lifestyle changes. Do not stop BP medicines suddenly or change them on your own. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Check blood pressure regularly at home or a clinic
Cut down on salt, pickles, papad and packaged/processed food
Exercise regularly and keep a healthy weight
Avoid smoking, tobacco and heavy alcohol
Manage stress and get enough sleep
warning_signs: Very severe headache with confusion or vision changes
Sudden weakness, numbness or trouble speaking
Blood pressure reading far above your usual range

name: Asthma
info: A long-term condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheezing, breathlessness and coughing. Triggers include dust, smoke, cold air, pollen, infections and exercise.
medicine_info: Asthma is treated with doctor-prescribed inhalers (a quick-relief inhaler and often a daily controller). Use them exactly as prescribed. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Identify and avoid triggers such as dust, smoke and strong smells
Keep your prescribed inhaler with you at all times
Keep bedding clean and avoid smoke, incense and mosquito coils indoors
Do not smoke and avoid second-hand smoke
Follow your doctor's asthma action plan
warning_signs: Unable to speak a full sentence because of breathlessness

name: Pneumonia
info: An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, usually bacterial or viral. It ranges from mild to life-threatening and is more serious in young children, older adults and people with other illnesses.
medicine_info: Pneumonia needs a doctor's assessment; antibiotics are prescribed only if the cause is bacterial. Do not self-treat with leftover antibiotics. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: See a doctor promptly for a proper diagnosis (often with a chest X-ray)
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Complete any prescribed treatment fully
Avoid smoking and smoky environments
Ask your doctor about pneumonia and flu vaccines for high-risk people
warning_signs: Chest pain that is getting worse

name: Acute Bronchitis
info: Inflammation of the airways (bronchial tubes), usually after a cold or flu virus. The main sign is a cough that may bring up mucus and can linger for a few weeks.
medicine_info: Most cases are viral and settle on their own, so antibiotics usually do not help. Honey-warm water, fluids and rest are common comfort measures. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Rest and drink plenty of warm fluids
Use steam inhalation or a humidifier
Avoid smoke, dust and strong fumes
Do not smoke
Wash hands often to avoid spreading infection

name: Tuberculosis (TB)
info: A bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs. It is curable with a full, supervised course of treatment.
medicine_info: TB must be diagnosed by tests (sputum test, chest X-ray). It is treated with a prescribed multi-drug course lasting many months — never stop early or skip doses. Free testing and treatment is available through government TB programmes. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get tested if a cough lasts more than 2 weeks
Cover your mouth when coughing and keep rooms ventilated
Take every dose of prescribed treatment for the full duration
Eat nutritious food and avoid smoking and alcohol
Household contacts should be screened
warning_signs: Missing doses or side effects such as yellow eyes or vomiting
Fever or cough returning during treatment

name: Dengue Fever
info: A mosquito-borne viral infection spread by the Aedes mosquito. It causes sudden high fever with severe body, joint and eye pain, and can drop platelet counts, so it needs monitoring.
medicine_info: There is no specific cure; treatment is supportive. Doctors usually advise paracetamol for fever and plenty of fluids. Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers in suspected dengue, as they can raise bleeding risk. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get a dengue test (NS1/IgM) and blood counts if fever with severe body pain occurs
Drink lots of fluids, ORS, coconut water and soups
Rest completely
Use mosquito nets/repellents and remove stagnant water around the home
Follow your doctor's advice on repeat blood tests
warning_signs: Severe stomach pain or persistent vomiting
Bleeding from the nose, gums, or blood in vomit/stool
Cold, clammy skin or extreme restlessness
Very drowsy or hard to wake
Fever dropping but you feel much worse (critical phase)

name: Malaria
info: A mosquito-borne parasitic infection spread by Anopheles mosquitoes. It typically causes fever with shivering and sweating that comes in cycles.
medicine_info: Malaria must be confirmed with a blood test (smear or rapid test); antimalarial medicines are prescribed by a doctor based on the type. Do not self-medicate. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get a malaria blood test promptly if fever with chills occurs
Sleep under a mosquito net and use repellents
Remove stagnant water near the home
Wear full-sleeved clothes in the evening
Finish the full prescribed course
warning_signs: Persistent vomiting so you cannot keep medicine down

name: Typhoid Fever
info: A bacterial infection (Salmonella Typhi) spread through contaminated food and water. Fever rises step by step over days, along with weakness and stomach upset.
medicine_info: Typhoid needs a blood test and a doctor-prescribed antibiotic course. Do not stop early or self-medicate. Rest and plenty of fluids and ORS help. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get a blood test (culture/Widal as advised) if fever lasts several days
Drink only boiled or safe, filtered water
Eat freshly cooked, hygienic food and avoid street food during illness
Wash hands with soap before eating and after the toilet
Ask your doctor about the typhoid vaccine
warning_signs: Severe stomach pain or swollen belly
Blood in stool or black stool
High fever not coming down despite treatment

name: COVID-19
info: A viral respiratory infection caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Illness ranges from mild cold-like symptoms to serious pneumonia, and a lost sense of smell or taste is a common clue.
medicine_info: Most mild cases recover with rest, fluids and fever/pain relief as advised by a doctor. Antiviral medicines are used only on a doctor's prescription. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Test (rapid antigen or RT-PCR) if you have symptoms
Isolate and wear a mask around others until recovered
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Monitor oxygen level with a pulse oximeter if available
Keep rooms ventilated and wash hands often
warning_signs: Confusion or inability to stay awake
Symptoms getting worse after a few days

name: Jaundice (Hepatitis)
info: Yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by excess bilirubin, often due to liver inflammation (hepatitis A/E from contaminated food and water), bile-duct blockage or blood disorders.
medicine_info: Jaundice needs a doctor's evaluation and liver tests to find the cause. Avoid self-medication, herbal remedies and alcohol, as many substances can strain the liver. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get liver function tests and a doctor's evaluation promptly
Drink boiled or safe water and eat fresh, light, low-oil food
Avoid alcohol and unnecessary medicines or herbal remedies
Rest and stay hydrated
Wash hands well to avoid spreading hepatitis A/E
warning_signs: Severe stomach pain or swelling of the belly
Symptoms worsening or lasting more than 2 weeks

name: Acid Reflux (GERD)
info: A condition where stomach acid flows back into the food pipe, causing heartburn and a sour taste. It is common and often triggered by large, oily or spicy meals and lying down soon after eating.
medicine_info: Antacids are commonly used for short-term relief. Stronger acid-reducing medicines should be taken only as advised by a doctor. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Eat smaller meals and avoid lying down for 2–3 hours after eating
Limit spicy, oily food, tea/coffee, soft drinks and alcohol
Raise the head of your bed slightly
Maintain a healthy weight and avoid smoking
Avoid tight clothing around the stomach
warning_signs: Chest pain with sweating, arm/jaw pain or breathlessness (could be a heart attack)
Symptoms not improving after a couple of weeks

name: Anemia
info: A condition in which the blood has too few red blood cells or too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen. Iron deficiency is the most common cause, especially in women, adolescents and pregnancy.
medicine_info: Treatment depends on the cause. Iron or vitamin supplements should be taken only after a blood test and a doctor's advice, since too much iron can be harmful. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Get a blood test (hemoglobin, ferritin) to find the cause
Eat iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, lentils, jaggery, dates and meat
Pair iron foods with vitamin C (lemon, amla, citrus fruit)
Avoid tea/coffee right after meals
Follow your doctor's advice on supplements and follow-up
warning_signs: Chest pain or very fast heartbeat

name: Chickenpox
info: A highly contagious viral infection (varicella-zoster) causing an itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters that crust over. It spreads easily through the air and by touching blisters.
medicine_info: Calamine lotion and cool baths can ease itching, and paracetamol may be used for fever as advised. Do not give aspirin to children. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Stay home and isolate until all blisters have crusted over
Keep nails short and avoid scratching to prevent scars and infection
Take cool baths and wear loose cotton clothing
Drink plenty of fluids
Keep away from newborns, pregnant women and people with weak immunity
warning_signs: Rash becoming red, hot, swollen or pus-filled (infection)
Severe headache, stiff neck or confusion

name: Kidney Stones
info: Hard mineral deposits that form in the kidneys and can cause sudden, severe, wave-like pain in the side or back as they move through the urinary tract.
medicine_info: Pain relief and medicines to help pass a stone are prescribed by a doctor after tests. Drinking plenty of water is the main home measure. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Drink plenty of water (enough for pale-yellow urine) throughout the day
Get an ultrasound or urine test as advised
Limit excess salt and very high-protein diets
Strain urine if your doctor asks you to catch the stone
Ask your doctor about diet changes based on stone type
warning_signs: Fever or chills with the pain (possible infection)
Pain so severe you cannot sit or lie still
Blood in urine that does not stop

name: Appendicitis
info: Inflammation of the appendix, a small pouch near the lower right abdomen. Pain often starts around the navel and then moves to the lower right side and worsens. It is a surgical emergency.
medicine_info: Do not take painkillers, laxatives or heat pads to 'treat' suspected appendicitis, as they can hide worsening or make it dangerous. Avoid eating or drinking until a doctor has examined you. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Go to a hospital emergency department the same day
Do not eat or drink until you have been examined
Do not use laxatives or heating pads
Do not rely on painkillers to mask the pain
Tell the doctor exactly where and when the pain started
warning_signs: Pain that suddenly gets much worse or spreads over the whole belly
Pain that worsens with walking, coughing or movement

name: Ear Infection
info: An infection of the middle or outer ear, common in children and after a cold. It causes ear pain, a feeling of blockage and sometimes fluid or pus coming from the ear.
medicine_info: Paracetamol is commonly used for pain as advised. Antibiotic ear drops or tablets are prescribed only by a doctor after examining the ear. Do not put oil, drops or objects in the ear unless advised. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Keep the ear dry while bathing and avoid swimming
Do not insert cotton buds, oil or drops unless your doctor says so
Use a warm (not hot) compress outside the ear for comfort
See a doctor if pain lasts more than 1–2 days
Complete any prescribed treatment
warning_signs: Pus or blood from the ear
Swelling or redness behind the ear

name: Ringworm (Fungal Skin Infection)
info: A common fungal infection of the skin (not a worm), producing ring-shaped, red, scaly, itchy patches. It spreads by touch and by sharing towels, clothes or combs, and thrives in sweaty, humid conditions.
medicine_info: Over-the-counter antifungal creams are commonly used for mild skin patches; a doctor may prescribe stronger creams or tablets. Avoid steroid creams unless a doctor advises, as they can worsen fungal infections. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Keep the skin clean and completely dry, especially skin folds
Do not share towels, clothes or combs
Wash clothes and bedding in hot water
Wear loose cotton clothing
Continue treatment for the full period even after the patch fades
warning_signs: Patches spreading fast or covering large areas
No improvement after 2 weeks of treatment

name: Scabies
info: A contagious skin condition caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin, causing intense itching (worse at night) and a rash, often between fingers, on wrists, waist and groin. It spreads by close contact.
medicine_info: Scabies is treated with a doctor-prescribed anti-scabies cream or lotion applied to the whole body as directed; close contacts usually need treatment too. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Treat all family members and close contacts at the same time
Wash bedding, towels and clothes in hot water and dry in sun/heat
Avoid scratching to prevent infection
Avoid skin contact with others until treated
Follow the full treatment schedule exactly
warning_signs: Sores with pus, warmth or spreading redness
Rash in infants or very elderly

name: Minor Cut (Laceration)
info: A break or slit in the skin from a knife, blade, glass or sharp edge. Small, shallow cuts usually heal well at home with proper cleaning.
medicine_info: Clean the wound and cover it with a sterile dressing; a topical antiseptic is commonly used. Pain relievers may be used for comfort as advised. Deep wounds may need stitches and a tetanus shot. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Wash your hands, then rinse the cut under clean running water for several minutes
Press firmly with a clean cloth for 5–10 minutes to stop bleeding
Clean around it with mild soap and cover with a sterile bandage
Change the dressing daily and keep it clean and dry
Make sure your tetanus vaccination is up to date (within about 5–10 years)
warning_signs: Bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
Cut is deep, gaping or longer than about 1 cm and may need stitches
Dirt, glass or rust stuck inside the wound
Redness, swelling, pus or warmth (infection) or fever
Numbness or inability to move the finger or limb

name: Scrape (Abrasion)
info: A superficial wound where the top layer of skin is rubbed off, often from a fall on a rough surface. It usually heals within a week or two.
medicine_info: Wash gently, apply a thin layer of antiseptic or antibiotic ointment, and cover with a non-stick dressing. Pain relievers may be used for comfort as advised. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Rinse with clean running water and remove loose dirt gently
Wash around the area with mild soap
Cover with a clean non-stick dressing
Change the dressing daily and keep it moist and clean
Make sure your tetanus vaccination is up to date
warning_signs: Gravel or dirt that will not wash out
Redness spreading, swelling, pus or fever
Large scrapes covering a big area
Bleeding that does not stop with pressure

name: Minor Burn
info: Skin damage from hot liquids, steam, hot oil, flames or hot surfaces. First-degree burns (red, painful, no blisters) and small second-degree burns (blisters) can be treated at home.
medicine_info: Cool running water is the first treatment. Aloe vera gel or a plain moisturizer may soothe healed skin; pain relievers may be used as advised. Do not apply toothpaste, butter, ghee, oil, ice or turmeric on a fresh burn. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Hold the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts
Cover loosely with a clean non-stick dressing or clean cling film
Do not burst blisters
Do not apply ice, toothpaste, butter, ghee, oil or powders
warning_signs: Burn larger than the palm of your hand, or on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a joint
Deep burn that looks white, charred or leathery
Burns from chemicals, electricity or inhaling smoke
Burns in infants, young children or older adults
Signs of infection such as pus, spreading redness or fever

name: Sprain
info: Stretching or tearing of ligaments around a joint, most often the ankle or wrist, after a twist or awkward fall. Swelling, pain and bruising are typical.
medicine_info: Pain relievers may be used as advised by a doctor or pharmacist. Rest, ice and compression are the main treatment. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Rest the joint and avoid putting weight on it
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours for the first day or two
Wrap with a compression bandage (snug, not tight)
Raise the injured limb above heart level when resting
Return to activity gradually once pain eases
warning_signs: Cannot bear weight or the joint looks deformed (could be a fracture)
Numbness, tingling or a cold, pale limb
Heard a pop or snap at the time of injury
Severe swelling or bruising right away

name: Suspected Fracture (Broken Bone)
info: A crack or break in a bone, usually after a fall, accident or heavy blow. It needs an X-ray and medical care to heal properly.
medicine_info: Do not self-treat a suspected fracture. A doctor will give pain relief and set or splint the bone. Avoid eating or drinking if surgery might be needed. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Keep the injured part still; do not try to straighten it
Support it with a splint or rolled newspaper/cloth and a sling
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling
Do not move the person if a head, neck or back injury is suspected
Go to a hospital for an X-ray
warning_signs: Bone visible through the skin or heavy bleeding
Limb looks bent, twisted or shortened
Numbness, tingling, cold or blue fingers/toes
Injury to head, neck or back
Severe pain or inability to move or bear weight

name: Dog / Animal Bite
info: A wound from a dog, cat, monkey or other animal. Even a small bite or scratch can carry rabies, tetanus or bacterial infection, so prompt washing and medical care matter.
medicine_info: There is no home cure. Rabies prevention (anti-rabies vaccine, and rabies immunoglobulin for severe bites) and tetanus protection are given by a doctor — start without delay, even if the animal looks healthy. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes
Apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine
Do not apply chilli, turmeric, oil or tie the wound tightly
Do not stitch or seal the wound tightly; let a doctor decide
Go to a hospital/clinic the same day for anti-rabies vaccination and tetanus protection
warning_signs: Bite to the face, head, neck, hands or genitals
Bite from a stray, wild or unknown animal, a bat or a monkey
Animal behaves strangely or dies/vanishes within 10 days

name: Snake Bite
info: A bite from a snake. Not all are venomous, but any snake bite should be treated as an emergency until a doctor says otherwise, because venom can cause bleeding, paralysis and breathing failure.
medicine_info: The only effective treatment for venomous snake bite is anti-snake venom given in a hospital. Do not use home or traditional remedies. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Go to the nearest hospital with anti-snake venom immediately — call emergency services
Keep the person calm and still; avoid walking
Immobilize the bitten limb like a fracture, keeping it at or slightly below heart level
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling begins
Do NOT cut, suck, burn, apply ice or herbs, or tie a tight tourniquet
warning_signs: Drooping eyelids, blurred vision or difficulty speaking or swallowing
Bleeding from gums, nose or the wound

name: Insect Bite or Sting
info: Bites or stings from mosquitoes, bees, wasps, ants, spiders or scorpions. Most cause only local pain, redness and itching, but some people have severe allergic reactions, and scorpion stings can be serious.
medicine_info: Cold compresses and calamine lotion can ease symptoms. Oral antihistamines or hydrocortisone cream are commonly used for itching or swelling as advised by a doctor or pharmacist. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Scrape out any visible bee sting with a flat edge (do not squeeze)
Wash with soap and water
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 10–15 minutes
Avoid scratching to prevent infection
Raise the limb if a hand or foot is swollen
warning_signs: Swelling of the lips, face or throat, wheeze or breathing difficulty (allergic reaction — emergency)
Dizziness, fainting or hives all over
Scorpion sting, especially in children — go to a hospital

name: Nosebleed
info: Bleeding from the nose, usually from small fragile blood vessels, often due to dry air, nose-picking, colds or minor knocks. Most nosebleeds are not serious.
medicine_info: Pressure is the main treatment. A thin layer of petroleum jelly inside the nostril can help keep it moist afterwards. Avoid decongestant nasal sprays unless advised. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Sit upright and lean slightly forward (do not tilt head back)
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 minutes without releasing
Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood
Apply a cold pack to the bridge of the nose
Avoid blowing or picking your nose for the next day or so
warning_signs: Bleeding lasting more than 20 minutes despite pressure
Nosebleed after a blow to the head or face
Heavy bleeding with dizziness or weakness
Nosebleeds while on blood thinners or with very high blood pressure

name: Bruise (Contusion)
info: A bruise forms when small blood vessels under the skin break after a bump or knock, causing a blue, purple or dark mark that fades through green and yellow over 1–2 weeks.
medicine_info: Cold packs in the first day or two and pain relievers as advised usually suffice. Gentle warmth after 48 hours can help it fade. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes, several times a day for the first 48 hours
Rest and raise the injured area
Avoid massaging the bruise early on
Use gentle warmth after 2 days
Avoid unnecessary aspirin or blood-thinning painkillers unless advised
warning_signs: Very large, painful or rapidly growing swelling
Bruises appearing without any injury or very easily
Bruise after a head injury with headache, vomiting or drowsiness
Numbness or inability to move the limb
Bruise that does not fade in 2–3 weeks

name: Puncture Wound (Nail / Thorn / Needle)
info: A small, deep, narrow wound from a nail, thorn, needle or sharp object. It may not bleed much but can push germs deep inside, so tetanus and infection are the main concerns.
medicine_info: Wash well and cover with a clean dressing. A tetanus shot is usually needed, especially for rusty or dirty objects; antibiotics are prescribed by a doctor if there is risk of infection. This is general information only, not a personal prescription — check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.
precautions: Wash with soap and running water for several minutes
Let it bleed a little (this helps flush out germs); stop heavy bleeding with pressure
Clean around it with an antiseptic and cover with a dry dressing
Check your tetanus vaccination and get a booster if due
Watch the wound closely for the next few days
warning_signs: Part of the object broken off or stuck inside
Deep wound to the foot, chest, abdomen or head
Redness spreading, swelling, throbbing, pus or fever
Jaw stiffness, muscle spasms or difficulty swallowing (possible tetanus)
Puncture from a rusty or dirty object with no recent tetanus shot
